 MR. WESSLER: Mr. Chief Justice, and
may it please the Court:
 ERISA's duty of prudence is inherently
 flexible.  As a result, this Court has
 consistently declined to inject judicially
 crafted bright-line rules into a determination
of whether a complaint's allegations plausibly
 allege imprudence.  Categorical rules, as this
Court put it colorfully in Dudenhoeffer, do not
 readily "divide the plausible sheep from the
meritless goats" because they are inconsistent
with the careful, context-sensitive inquiry
that both ERISA and Rule 8 require.
 The Ninth Circuit's "meaningful
benchmark requirement" is just such a rule.
Under it, a court first asks whether a

own can plausibly demonstrate imprudence by
identifying a virtually indistinguishable fund
 that performed better.  If the complaint fails
to identify that specific fund, the performance
 allegations are discarded, and that is true
even if the complaint relies on benchmarks
 selected by the fiduciaries themselves or
 comparators identified by benchmarking experts.
 In the Respondents' view, this rule is
 consistent with the ordinary pleading framework
set forth in Twombly and Iqbal. But, under
that framework, courts must assess all
 non-conclusory allegations together in
determining if a complaint plausibly states a
 claim. The "meaningful benchmark requirement"
 precludes that assessment.
 And the Ninth Circuit's rule isn't
 even necessary.  Everyone agrees that, without
 more, a complaint merely alleging that one fund
 performed better than another won't survive a
 motion to dismiss.  The ordinary pleading
standards, however, are perfectly capable of
weeding out a truly meritorious --meritless
 claim like that.
